title: Portfolio
summary: This portfolio presents my résumé and projects while serving as a frontend work sample for interaction design, state management, accessibility, and content architecture. I built windows, folders, a Dock, and a terminal in the browser, then connected URLs, browser history, keyboard interaction, and preferences into one experience.

projectIntro.title: Project overview
projectIntro.description:
I designed a Korean/English portfolio that lets visitors explore both a terminal and an OS-style GUI in the browser. Career and Resume share the same career, skills, and contact data, while localized content and UI labels are managed separately. Language, wallpaper, and Dock preferences persist across reloads.

Visitors can open and switch applications by keyboard, with distinct focus and selection states. Playwright checks cover opening project windows, keeping windows within screen bounds, removing their DOM elements after closing, and switching applications by keyboard.

ownership.title: I separated the GUI shell from product features by why they change.
ownership.description: Windows, the Dock, folders, and browser navigation belong to the OS runtime, while Terminal, Portfolio, Guestbook, and Settings own their screens and user flows.

problem.description: When OS UI code and application features live at the same layer, changing window behavior requires inspecting product screens and features start to depend directly on the GUI store.

decision.description: I placed GuiShell, windows, the Dock, directories, navigation, and the store in src/app/gui, and kept each application screen and user flow in src/features. For Terminal, Guestbook, and Settings, adapters inject GUI state as props so features do not import the GUI store directly.

result.description: The path alone now makes it clear whether the OS runtime or a product feature owns a concern. GUI changes and app changes move independently instead of reaching into each other's internal implementation.

appContract.title: I split app registration into file-level contracts.
appContract.description: Adding an app takes more than creating a window. Its title, URL, dynamic loading, folder presence, and browser navigation must agree on the same app ID.

problem.description: App metadata, component loading, the directory tree, and URL handling live in separate files. Missing one can leave an app visible in the Dock but unopened, or prevent a shared URL from restoring it.

decision.description: appCatalog.ts holds only serializable metadata that the server can read, while appLoaderRegistry.tsx holds client-only dynamic imports. directoryTree.ts references catalog app IDs. planNavigation.ts calculates state changes and URL effects as a pure function, and GuiNavigationProvider is the only caller of the History API.

result.description:
I separated static app metadata, client-only loaders, folder nodes, and browser navigation into files with distinct responsibilities. Types check the relationship between app IDs and props, while structure checks and unit tests verify consistency across the app catalog, loaders, URLs, folder nodes, and localized title keys.

Tests also check that shared URL normalization, user navigation, and back navigation follow the same navigation plan. They cover how popstate events from browser history changes update the GUI state.

architecture.title: Folder and runtime structure of the OS-style portfolio
architecture.description: The route entry composes the GUI runtime, the GUI shell manages windows and navigation, and each feature owns an independent application screen and user flow.
